title: Secrets in the source
brief: 17:00. A contractor asks for read access to the portal repository. Before you grant it, you check what is in the code.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: Anyone who can read the repository can read the production database password.
teaches: A secret in code is a secret shared with everyone who ever sees the repository
Read secrets from the environment or a secrets manager, and rotate any that leaked
Deleting the line does not remove it from history; scanning stops it happening again

value.title: Portal repository: config review
value.intro: Search the repository the way a new contractor could, then see if what you find works.

attempts.label: Search the repository for "password"
attempts.response:
portal/config/db.js:4:  password: 'Tr0ub4dor&Prod!',

A production password, in plain text, readable by every collaborator.

attempts.label: Try that password on the production database
attempts.response:
CONNECTED to portal_prod

The password from the repository still works.
attempts.fixedResponse:
FATAL: password authentication failed for user "portal_app"

The old password has been rotated.

fix.step: Pick the fix that closes the hole
fix.prompt: Pick every step needed, including the one that deals with the password that is already exposed.

options.label: Read the password from the environment or a secrets manager
code: + password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD,   // injected at deploy time
options.why: The code no longer contains the secret, so reading the code does not give it away.

options.label: Rotate the production password now, because it has already been exposed
code: + ALTER ROLE portal_app WITH PASSWORD '<new, generated, stored in the secrets manager>';
options.why: A secret that has been in a repository has to be treated as leaked. Only rotation makes the old one useless.

options.label: Add secret scanning to commits and CI so it cannot happen again
options.why: Catches the next one before it is pushed, and finds the ones already in history.

options.label: Delete the line in a new commit
options.why: The password is still in every earlier commit, and in every clone. Deleting a line does not delete history.

options.label: Store the password base64 encoded
options.why: Encoding is not encryption. Anyone can decode it in one command.

setup.title: Workbench
setup.body: Check the repo before granting access

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: Anyone who can read the repository can read the production database password.

label: Send this request: it breaks it
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: A search for the word password found the production database password, and it connected. Anyone with read access, including contractors, past staff and any tool that ever cloned the repository, could do the same.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: One search, one working password
body: A search for the word password found the production database password, and it connected. Anyone with read access, including contractors, past staff and any tool that ever cloned the repository, could do the same.
The TODO comment says it all: “move this”.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

label: Untick this one, it does not fix the cause
Pick this change
Picked everything that fixes it? Apply the patch
Open the Fix tab

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: The secret now lives outside the repository. The old one is rotated so it is worthless, and scanning means the next one is caught before it is pushed.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Out of the code, out of use, out of future commits
body: The secret now lives outside the repository. The old one is rotated so it is worthless, and scanning means the next one is caught before it is pushed.
Rotation is the step people skip. The password was exposed, so it is over.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Removing the line or encoding the value leaves the password in history and in every clone, and encoding is not protection. The exposed password still opens the database.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: Deleted from the file, not from the world
body: Removing the line or encoding the value leaves the password in history and in every clone, and encoding is not protection. The exposed password still opens the database.
Move it out, rotate it, and scan.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

label: Send the exploit again: it should be blocked
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
